samples.text:
Today countries trade with each other more than ever before, and food can be imported easily from all over the world. Some people believe that because of this, it is not necessary for each country to produce enough food for its own people. I disagree with this idea.

The main reason is that depending on other countries for food is risky. If there is a war, a natural disaster or a political problem, the imports can stop suddenly. For example, during the pandemic, many countries closed their borders and some food products became very expensive or difficult to find in the shops. If a country cannot produce its own food, its people can suffer from hunger in this kind of situation.

Another reason is that farming gives jobs to many people, especially in the countryside. If a country buy all its food from abroad, the farmers will lose their jobs and they will move to the cities to find work. This can make the cities more crowded and the villages will become empty. Also, the traditional way of life in rural areas will disappear.

On the other hand, it is true that some countries cannot produce all their food because they have a dry climate or not enough land. For them, import is necessary and it can be cheaper. But I think they should still try to produce the most important foods, such as rice or wheat, as much as possible.

In conclusion, I do not agree that it is no longer necessary for countries to produce enough food for their people. Although import is useful, every country should try to be independent in food so that they are safe in difficult times.

samples.text:
Global trade has made it possible for countries to import food from almost anywhere, leading some to argue that national self-sufficiency in food is no longer necessary. I partly agree with this view: complete self-sufficiency is unrealistic and often inefficient, but I believe every country should still maintain a significant capacity to feed its population.

It is true that international trade brings important benefits. Countries differ greatly in climate, soil and water resources, and it makes economic sense for each to specialise in what it can produce most efficiently. A desert nation that tried to grow all its own grain would waste enormous amounts of water and money, whereas importing it from countries with fertile land is far cheaper. Trade also gives consumers access to a wider variety of food throughout the year, and it can help stabilise supplies when one region experiences a poor harvest.

However, relying heavily on imports leaves a country vulnerable to events beyond its control. Wars, trade disputes and pandemics can disrupt supply chains suddenly, and in recent years export bans by major producers have caused sharp price rises for staple foods in many importing countries. Poorer nations are particularly exposed, as they may be unable to compete for limited supplies when global prices increases. In such situations, a strong domestic farming sector can act as essential insurance.

Furthermore, agriculture supports rural employment and communities, and abandoning it entirely could lead to economic decline in the countryside and the loss of valuable farming knowledge.

For these reasons, I believe the sensible approach is a balance: countries should trade for food where it is efficient, but ensure that they can produce enough of their basic staples, or hold sufficient reserves, to cope with a crisis.

In conclusion, although globalisation means that total self-sufficiency is no longer essential, I do not think countries can safely abandon domestic food production altogether.

samples.text:
The expansion of global trade has transformed how food reaches our tables, and some now argue that national food self-sufficiency has become an outdated goal. I agree that complete self-sufficiency is neither necessary nor, for many countries, achievable. However, I disagree with the broader implication that nations can safely neglect their capacity to feed themselves.

There is a strong economic logic to relying on trade. Agricultural conditions vary enormously, and forcing every country to grow all its own food would be highly inefficient. Arid or densely populated states would need to divert scarce water and land to crops that can be produced far more cheaply elsewhere, raising prices for their own citizens. Open markets allow resources to be used where they are most productive and can cushion the impact of a failed harvest in any one region by drawing on supplies from others.

Yet the assumption that global markets will always function smoothly is a dangerous one. Food supply chains are long and interdependent, and they have repeatedly proved fragile in the face of conflict, extreme weather and pandemics. When supplies tighten, exporting countries often prioritise their own populations by restricting sales abroad, precisely when importers need them most. Nations with weak domestic production and limited purchasing power are the first to suffer, and food shortages can quickly lead to social unrest.

Climate change is likely to heighten these risks, as droughts and floods disrupt harvests in major producing regions more frequently. In this context, maintaining a viable farming sector, diversifying import sources and holding strategic reserves are prudent forms of insurance rather than economic nationalism.

In conclusion, globalisation has made total self-sufficiency unnecessary, but it has not removed the need for food security. Each country should aim for sufficient domestic capacity and resilience to withstand disruption, even if it continues to rely on trade for much of what it consumes.
samples.why: Nuanced, precisely stated position · ideas fully extended and logically sequenced · effective cohesion and paragraphing · wide, accurate vocabulary · varied complex structures with no noticeable errors.
